title: Secrets: Store Passwords and API Keys Safely

chapters.title: Secrets: Store Passwords and API Keys Safely
chapters.subtitle: Keep passwords and API keys encrypted, in one list

steps.text: Every site depends on sensitive values, such as a mail password or a payment API key. The Secrets module keeps them encrypted, in one list. In this video, you create, review, replace, delete, and use secrets.

chapters.title: Why keep secrets together
chapters.subtitle: The problem the Secrets module solves

steps.text: Passwords and API keys often end up in configuration files, settings pages, and shared notes. Each copy can leak, and nothing lists the keys a site uses or the ones about to expire.
The Secrets module gives each value a name and encrypts it before saving. One list shows every secret, its type, where it is kept, and when it expires. Settings then refer to a secret by name.

chapters.title: Turn on the Secrets feature
chapters.subtitle: Enable it and find its pages

steps.text: The Secrets module is a feature that you turn on. Open Tools, Features, and search for Secrets.
Select Enable next to Secrets, and a message confirms that the feature was enabled.
Its pages are under Tools, Security: Secrets, Migrate Secrets, and Secret Stores. Let's open Secrets.
The list is empty. Add Secret creates the first secret.

chapters.title: Create a text secret
chapters.subtitle: A password or an API key

steps.text: Select Add Secret. A dialog asks for the type of secret: Text Secret, RSA Key, or X.509 Certificate.
A Text Secret holds a value such as a password, an API key, or a connection string. Let's store the password of the mail account that sends this site's email.
Select Create under Text Secret, and enter a name. Settings refer to the secret by this name, so it cannot be changed later.
The Store field shows Database, where the secret is kept. The value is a password field: it is encrypted when saved, and never displayed again.
Add a description so others know what the secret is for. The expiration date is optional and does not disable the secret: it reminds you to replace the value in time.
Select Save. A message confirms the creation, and the list shows the secret with badges for its type, store, expiration, and last update.
An RSA Key secret holds a key pair that Orchard Core generates for you. Select Add Secret, then Create under RSA Key. Enter a name, choose a key size of 2048, 3072, or 4096 bits, and save.
Once saved, the private key is never shown, and the key pair cannot be changed. Only the description and expiration date can be edited.

An X.509 Certificate secret has two sources. Certificate store refers to a certificate installed on the server, by thumbprint. PEM-encoded certificate keeps the certificate text itself, with an optional private key.
The Secrets list shows each name, description, and badges. A warning above the list counts the secrets that have expired or expire within 30 days.
Secrets that have expired, or expire within 30 days, are highlighted. An expired secret keeps working: the highlight is a reminder to replace its value.
Type in the search box and press Enter to find secrets by name, description, type, or store.
The Expiration filter shows expired secrets, secrets that expire within 30 days, or secrets that never expire. The Type filter shows the secrets of one type.
People who can view secrets also see this warning on the admin home page, with a Review secrets link.
To replace a value, such as a renewed key, select Edit next to the secret. The Value field is empty, because stored values are never displayed. Leave it empty to keep the current value.
Enter the replacement value, and set a later expiration date. Select Save, and this secret is no longer counted in the expiration warning.

chapters.title: Delete secrets
chapters.subtitle: One at a time, or several at once

steps.text: To delete a secret, select Delete next to it and confirm. Features that refer to a deleted secret can no longer read its value, so check where it is used first.
To delete several secrets at once, select them, open the Actions menu, and choose Delete. After you confirm, a message reports how many secrets were deleted.

chapters.title: Use a secret in settings
chapters.subtitle: Select a secret instead of typing a value

steps.text: Settings pages that need a password or a key let you pick a secret instead of typing the value. Let's open Settings, Communication, Email, and the SMTP tab.
Check Enable SMTP Provider, enter a sender email address and a host name, and check Require credentials. The User name and Password fields appear.
The Password field asks where the value is kept. User-specified value encrypts the password you type, and keeps it with these settings. Use a secret refers to a secret by name.
Choose Use a secret, and pick it from the list. If the secret is missing, New secret opens the secret editor in another tab, and the reload button refreshes the list.
Select Save. A message confirms the update, and SMTP reads its password from the secret. Saving with a secret removes any password stored in these settings.
The settings of email, SMS, Google, GitHub, Microsoft, Meta, X (Twitter), OpenID Connect clients, and Azure AI Search use this same editor for their credentials.

Two permissions control access. View secrets lists secrets without their values, and Manage secrets also adds, edits, moves, and deletes them. Administrators have both; assign them to other roles under Access Control, Roles.
Two more pages are under Tools, Security. Migrate Secrets moves credentials that settings already hold into secrets, and Secret Stores moves secrets between stores. A separate video covers both.

steps.text: That is the Secrets module: passwords and API keys kept encrypted, listed in one place, and referenced by name from your settings. Thanks for watching.
